newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu vows to shield settlement on U.S. trip.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu vows to shield settlement on U.S. trip.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Thursday ahead of a meeting next week with U.S. President Bill Clinton not to relinquish a right to settle Jews in occupied lands.

Jewish settlers mobilised to stiffen the prime minister's resolve in the face of news reports Clinton would press him at the meeting on Monday to freeze settlement construction as part of a package to revive crumbling peace talks with the PLO.
The Israeli reports, quoting unidentified U.S. officials, said the United States would also push Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to order a clampdown on militants.

"The prime minister will make clear in Washington that Israel stands by its right to build in Jerusalem and in settlements, and included in that the building will continue at Har Homa," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said.
Arabs insist peace talks should be renewed only when Israel halts work on a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on a hill called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

Palestinians say the settlement pre-empts future talks on the status of East Jerusalem, seized by Israel in 1967 and claimed by both sides. Daily violence has replaced Israeli-PLO dialogue since Netanyahu broke ground on March 18.
The Israeli leader has said that the Jewish state will not resume peacemaking until Arafat cracks down on "terrorism".

Netanyahu says Arafat gave Islamist militants a green light to launch attacks such as a suicide bombing that killed three Israelis two weeks ago and a pair of botched suicide attacks in Gaza this week.
The military wing of the Islamic Jihad group on Thursday claimed responsibility for the Gaza attacks. Jihad sources said the Palestinian Authority had arrested 30 of their activists.
Netanyahu's office said Israel had suspended its request to extradite Moussa Abu Marzook, a politburo member of the militant Islamic group Hamas, from the United States.

Security sources said Israel feared that the extradition of Abu Marzook, who in January stopped fighting a 1995 Israeli extradition request, would spark a wave of attacks in the Jewish state and harm its struggle against Islamist groups.
All eyes have turned to Middle East peace sponsor Washington to put forward a new initiative. Clinton has pledged renewed personal involvement to put peace moves back on track.

Before meeting Clinton in Washington, Netanayahu will visit Jordan's King Hussein on Sunday in Minnesota, where the monarch is to undergo surgery. King Hussein met Clinton and held talks with senior U.S. officials in Washington this week.
Jewish settlers, who helped propel Netanyahu to power last year, urged the right-wing prime minister not to give in to "terrorism" by agreeing to a settlement freeze.
"The fixed ritual that concessions are needed in order to stop acts of murder will lead to more acts of terror," the YESHA Jewish settler council wrote in a letter to Netanyahu.
YESHA said it also sent a letter to U.S. Ambassador Martin Indyk protesting "the U.S. president's intention to dictate to the Israeli government" on its settlement policy.
Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan denied an Israeli Channel Two television report that Israel had recently approved construction of thousands of new homes for Jews in the West Bank.
